answer.rationale: The incumbent has already refused to reopen price this cycle, which forecloses negotiate_terms. Defer_decision is not viable because the contract expires in 14 days with no auto-renew, so deferral would leave the assembly line without supply and introduce immediate delivery risk. Add_second_source does not by itself reduce cost; it mitigates risk but does not address the 18% spend cut. That leaves renew_incumbent or switch_primary_vendor. Renew_incumbent preserves integration stability (memory_c1) but does not move cost down, and memory_c6 shows multi-year commitments only unlock volume pricing when the incumbent is willing to negotiate, which they have explicitly refused. Memory_c2 records that the low-cost vendor was already onboarded last year, invoicing was accurate, and unit cost fell sharply, so the migration risk and onboarding cost that normally argue against a switch have already been absorbed. Given the primary objective is to minimize total cost of ownership without increasing delivery risk, switching to the already-proven low-cost vendor is the only direction that directly meets the 18% finance mandate while keeping delivery performance on known footing. Flagging downstream value risk: the assembly line is at 94% committed volume with no buffer, so the switchover must be staged within the 14-day window rather than a hard cutover, and the incumbent is held as a fallback during transition. One memory is being verified (memory_c2) because the switch depends on the low-cost vendor's onboarding and invoicing performance being as favorable as the summary suggests; if the archived record contradicts that, I would fall back to renew_incumbent at current terms and revisit cost reduction next cycle.
